INJURY AND ILLNESS PREVENTION PROGRAM (IIPP) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

ABOUT THIS IIPP INFORMATION SHEET
This Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet describes California's statutory requirement that every employer establish, implement, and maintain a written injury prevention program, set out in Labor Code § 6401.7, and the implementing Cal/OSHA regulation that specifies the program's required written elements, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between Jordan Lee and Acme Innovations LLC.

It summarizes selected requirements of that statute and regulation: the statute's own list of required program elements, who must be identified as having authority and responsibility for the program, what triggers a hazard evaluation and how identified hazards must be corrected, when employee training is required, what records must be kept and how an employee may access the written program, and how the program is enforced, including the statute's own safe harbor for an employer that adopts Cal/OSHA's model program.

Acme Innovations LLC has identified Pat Morgan as the person with authority and responsibility for implementing its Program.

This information sheet is not itself Acme Innovations LLC's written Injury and Illness Prevention Program, does not itself satisfy Labor Code § 6401.7's or 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203's written-program requirement, and does not determine that any particular practice of Acme Innovations LLC's is or is not compliant with California law.

THE STATUTORY DUTY TO ESTABLISH A WRITTEN PROGRAM
California Labor Code § 6401.7(a) itself states that every employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective injury prevention program, that the program shall be written (except for a narrower class of employers addressed in subdivision (e)), and that the written program shall include, but is not limited to, a list of elements the statute itself enumerates: identification of the person or persons responsible for implementing the program; a system for identifying and evaluating workplace hazards, including scheduled periodic inspections; methods and procedures for correcting unsafe or unhealthy conditions in a timely manner; an occupational health and safety training program; a system for communicating with employees on safety matters without fear of reprisal; a system for ensuring employee compliance with safe work practices; and, as of a 2024 amendment, a workplace violence prevention plan conforming to the separate requirements of Labor Code § 6401.9. Subdivision (e)(1) then directs the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board to adopt a regulation setting forth the employer's duties under the section, consistent with the requirements the statute specifies in subdivisions (a) through (d). That regulation is 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, addressed in the companion clauses of this information sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Every employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective injury prevention program. The program shall be written, except as provided in subdivision (e), and shall include, but not be limited to, the following elements:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  "The standards board shall adopt a standard setting forth the employer’s duties under this section, on or before January 1, 1991, consistent with the requirements specified in subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (d)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (e)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  Known gap: The statute itself is not a bare delegation to Cal/OSHA — it enumerates the program's required elements in subdivision (a) and separately directs the standards board to adopt an implementing regulation 'consistent with' subdivisions (a) through (d), rather than leaving the entire content of the program to the regulation to invent. Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same enacted statute, Labor Code § 6401.7 — different subdivisions of one section, not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently verify Labor Code § 6401.9 (the workplace violence prevention plan requirement subdivision (a)(7) now cross-references) or the small-employer and low-hazard-industry modifications in subdivision (e); those are named here only as topics the statute itself flags, not as verified content, and are omitted from the citations below rather than summarized as fact. This is a description of what one state's statute requires, not a claim about what any particular employer has or has not done.

IDENTIFYING WHO HAS AUTHORITY AND RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE PROGRAM
Both the statute and its implementing regulation require a written Injury and Illness Prevention Program to identify who is responsible for it, though they phrase the requirement slightly differently. Labor Code § 6401.7(a)(1) requires 'identification of the person or persons responsible for implementing the program.' The implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(a)(1), requires the written program to 'identify the person or persons with authority and responsibility for implementing the Program' — adding 'authority' to the statute's 'responsibility.' Neither source requires that this person hold any particular job title, such as 'safety officer' or 'safety coordinator'; both allow more than one person to be identified. Acme Innovations LLC has identified Pat Morgan as the person with authority and responsibility for implementing its Program.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Identification of the person or persons responsible for implementing the program."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  "(1) Identify the person or persons with authority and responsibility for implementing the Program."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  Known gap: The regulation's phrase — 'authority and responsibility' — is not a verbatim restatement of the statute's phrase — 'responsible for implementing.' This clause draws on two formally distinct primary sources: Labor Code § 6401.7, enacted by the Legislature, and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, adopted by the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board under authority the statute itself confers in subdivision (e)(1); they are independent legal instruments even though the regulation implements the statute. Neither source was found to require a specific job title, credential, or minimum authority level for the person identified, beyond the words quoted here.

WHEN HAZARD EVALUATION IS REQUIRED AND HOW HAZARDS MUST BE CORRECTED
The implementing regulation requires the written program to include procedures for identifying and evaluating workplace hazards, including scheduled periodic inspections to identify unsafe conditions and work practices, and it specifies three triggering events for such an inspection or evaluation: when the program is first established; whenever new substances, processes, procedures, or equipment are introduced to the workplace that represent a new occupational safety and health hazard; and whenever the employer is made aware of a new or previously unrecognized hazard. The regulation's own text requires that these be 'scheduled periodic inspections,' without stating a specific numeric interval (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually) at which they must recur. Once a hazard is identified, the regulation separately requires methods or procedures for correcting unsafe or unhealthy conditions, work practices, and work procedures in a timely manner based on the severity of the hazard, and, for an imminent hazard that cannot be immediately abated without endangering employees or property, it requires removing all exposed personnel from the area except those necessary to correct the condition, who must be provided the necessary safeguards. The statute itself states the same timely-correction duty at the statutory level, separately from the regulation's more detailed treatment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(4) Include procedures for identifying and evaluating work place hazards including scheduled periodic inspections to identify unsafe conditions and work practices. Inspections shall be made to identify and evaluate hazards:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(4) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  "(B) Whenever new substances, processes, procedures, or equipment are introduced to the workplace that represent a new occupational safety and health hazard; and"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(4)(B) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  "(B) When an imminent hazard exists which cannot be immediately abated without endangering employee(s) and/or property, remove all exposed personnel from the area except those necessary to correct the existing condition. Employees necessary to correct the hazardous condition shall be provided the necessary safeguards."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(6)(B) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  "The employer shall correct unsafe and unhealthy conditions and work practices in a timely manner based on the severity of the hazard."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  Known gap: This corrects an assumption that the regulation fixes a specific inspection frequency, such as an annual or quarterly schedule — the regulatory text located and quoted here does not state one; it requires only that inspections be 'scheduled periodic inspections' tied to the three triggering events quoted above, leaving the specific interval for the employer's own program to set. The three subsections of this clause drawn from the hazard-identification and hazard-correction requirements — subdivisions (a)(4) and (a)(6) — are both part of the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, and are not independent of each other; the statutory quotation is drawn from a separate, independent source, Labor Code § 6401.7, though it states only the general correction duty and not the regulation's inspection triggers or its imminent-hazard removal procedure. This is a statement of what the regulation and statute require in general, not a claim about whether any specific inspection or correction has occurred.

WHEN EMPLOYEE TRAINING IS REQUIRED
Labor Code § 6401.7(c) itself requires the employer to train all employees when the training program is first established, all new employees, and all employees given a new job assignment, and to train employees whenever new substances, processes, procedures, or equipment are introduced to the workplace and represent a new hazard, or whenever the employer receives notification of a new or previously unrecognized hazard. The implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(a)(7), requires the written program to 'provide training and instruction' and lists the same triggering events in more granular form — first establishment of the program, new employees, employees given a new job assignment for which training has not previously been received, new substances/processes/procedures/equipment representing a new hazard, and a newly recognized hazard — and it adds one requirement the statutory text quoted here does not separately spell out: training for supervisors specifically, so that supervisors familiarize themselves with the safety and health hazards to which the employees under their immediate direction and control may be exposed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The employer shall train all employees when the training program is first established, all new employees, and all employees given a new job assignment, and shall train employees whenever new substances, processes, procedures, or equipment are introduced to the workplace and represent a new hazard, and whenever the employer receives notification of a new or previously unrecognized hazard."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  "(7) Provide training and instruction:"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(7) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  "(F) For supervisors to familiarize themselves with the safety and health hazards to which employees under their immediate direction and control may be exposed."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(7)(F) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  Known gap: The regulation's supervisor-specific training item, subdivision (a)(7)(F), is not a restatement of anything found in the statutory text of § 6401.7(c) quoted here — the statute's own text speaks only of training 'employees' and does not use the word 'supervisor.' This clause draws on two independent primary sources — the enacted statute and the standards board's implementing regulation — rather than restating one source's language as though it appeared in both.

RECORDKEEPING AND EMPLOYEE ACCESS TO THE PROGRAM
Labor Code § 6401.7(d) itself requires the employer to keep appropriate records of the steps taken to implement and maintain the program. The implementing regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(b), specifies two categories those records must include: records of the scheduled and periodic inspections required by subdivision (a)(4), including who conducted the inspection, the unsafe conditions and work practices identified, and the action taken to correct them, which must be maintained for at least one year; and documentation of the safety and health training required by subdivision (a)(7) for each employee, including the employee's name or other identifier, training dates, the type of training, and the training providers, also maintained for at least one year. Separately, subdivision (a)(8) of the regulation requires the employer to allow an employee access to the Program, and subdivision (a)(8)(B)(1) requires that access be provided in a reasonable time, place, and manner, but in no event later than five business days after the employer receives a request for access from an employee or a designated representative.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The employer shall keep appropriate records of steps taken to implement and maintain the program."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  "(1) Records of scheduled and periodic inspections required by subsection (a)(4) to identify unsafe conditions and work practices, including person(s) conducting the inspection, the unsafe conditions and work practices that have been identified and action taken to correct the identified unsafe conditions and work practices. These records shall be maintained for at least one (1) year; and"
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (b)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  "(2) Documentation of safety and health training required by subsection (a)(7) for each employee, including employee name or other identifier, training dates, type(s) of training, and training providers. This documentation shall be maintained for at least one (1) year."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (b)(2) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  "1. Provide access in a reasonable time, place, and manner, but in no event later than five (5) business days after the request for access is received from an employee or designated representative."
  — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3203, subd. (a)(8)(B)(1) (https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/3203.html)
  Known gap: The one-year retention period and the five-business-day access deadline are both regulatory requirements found in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, not language found in the statutory text of Labor Code § 6401.7(d) quoted here, which states only a general duty to keep 'appropriate records' without specifying a retention period. The three regulatory subsections cited in this clause — (b)(1), (b)(2), and (a)(8)(B)(1) — are all part of the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, and are not independent of one another or of the other clauses of this information sheet that also cite that regulation; the statutory quotation is drawn from the separate, independent source, Labor Code § 6401.7. This document did not independently verify the regulation's further exceptions for employers with fewer than 10 or fewer than 20 employees, which shorten or modify some of these recordkeeping obligations; those exceptions are not summarized here and no citation is offered for their specific terms.

ENFORCEMENT AND THE MODEL PROGRAM SAFE HARBOR
Neither the text of Labor Code § 6401.7 nor the text of 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 quoted in this information sheet states a specific civil penalty amount for a violation. Section 6401.7(j)(1) does, however, confirm that a violation of the section is enforced through a 'citation' process and can carry a 'civil penalty': it directs the Division of Occupational Safety and Health to prepare a Model Injury and Illness Prevention Program for Non-High-Hazard Employment and make it available to employers on request, and it provides that an employer who adopts and implements that model program in good faith shall not be assessed a civil penalty for the first citation for a violation of the section issued after the employer's adoption and implementation of the model program.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The division shall prepare a Model Injury and Illness Prevention Program for Non-High-Hazard Employment, and shall make copies of the model program prepared pursuant to this subdivision available to employers, upon request, for posting in the workplace. An employer who adopts and implements the model program prepared by the division pursuant to this paragraph in good faith shall not be assessed a civil penalty for the first citation for a violation of this section issued after the employer’s adoption and implementation of the model program."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 6401.7 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. Code § 6401.7, subd. (j)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=6401.7.)
  Known gap: This clause corrects an assumption that § 6401.7 itself states a penalty schedule or dollar figure for a violation — the statutory text located and quoted here does not; it establishes only a first-citation safe harbor tied to good-faith adoption of the Division's model program, and its wording ('citation,' 'civil penalty') presupposes that the general Cal/OSHA citation and civil-penalty framework — found elsewhere in the Labor Code and in Cal/OSHA's own citation regulations, not in § 6401.7 or § 3203 themselves — is what actually sets citation classifications and penalty amounts for a violation of this section. This document did not independently fetch or verify that separate citation-and-penalty framework, so no citation or quotation is offered for it here, and it should not be inferred from anything quoted in this information sheet. This clause's quotation is drawn from the same statute, Labor Code § 6401.7, cited in the other clauses of this information sheet, not from an independent second source.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

Program Administrator: Pat Morgan
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme Innovations LLC:

citations.quote: The division shall prepare a Model Injury and Illness Prevention Program for Non-High-Hazard Employment, and shall make copies of the model program prepared pursuant to this subdivision available to employers, upon request, for posting in the workplace. An employer who adopts and implements the model program prepared by the division pursuant to this paragraph in good faith shall not be assessed a civil penalty for the first citation for a violation of this section issued after the employer’s adoption and implementation of the model program.
